standard.title: Create evidence-based civic arguments
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate evidence
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence (AC9HC8S05). At Year 9 the expectation advances from referencing to incorporating evidence — evidence should be integrated into the argument structure rather than added as a gesture.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and arguments using civics and citizenship knowledge, concepts and terms, with evidence incorporated into the argument structure.

nodes.label: Using civic concepts and terms accurately
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can accurately apply civics and citizenship concepts and terms in their written or oral responses.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least three civics and citizenship terms accurately in a written or oral response on a civic topic.
nodes.typical_width: Use civics and citizenship concepts and terms accurately in descriptions, explanations and arguments, including terms such as 'representative', 'jurisdictions', 'parliamentary majority', 'mandate', 'precedent', 'presumption of innocence'; demonstrate understanding of the term through accurate application rather than definition alone.
wider: Practise using civic concepts and terms in varied contexts — applying the same term in different argument types (description, explanation, evaluation) to build flexible understanding
Examine how civic concepts are used (and sometimes misused) in media and political discourse, and evaluate the implications for public understanding
Build a personal civics glossary with examples of correct use drawn from real civic sources such as court judgements, parliamentary debate or policy documents

response_modes.reason: Accurate use of civic terminology requires regular, low-stakes application across multiple contexts. Students who are only exposed to terms in definition exercises often misapply them in extended writing — deliberate practice in varied written tasks builds accuracy.

success_criteria: Uses at least three civics and citizenship terms accurately in context
The terms are applied to demonstrate understanding, not simply defined

nodes.label: Incorporating evidence into civic arguments
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct a civic argument in which evidence is incorporated into the argument structure, not merely appended.
nodes.minimum_width: Construct an argument on a civic issue that includes at least one piece of evidence integrated into the body of the argument (not just listed at the end).
nodes.typical_width: Develop an evidence-based argument about a civics and citizenship issue — such as a need to reform youth justice arrangements in a particular jurisdiction; incorporate evidence into the argument structure by using it to support claims, acknowledge counter-arguments, and draw conclusions; use civic concepts and terms throughout.
wider: Develop arguments on the same civic issue from opposing perspectives, and evaluate which argument makes more effective use of evidence
Construct an argument that responds to a counter-argument — specifically addressing contrary evidence rather than ignoring it

Develop a multimodal civic argument (written, visual, or oral) for a specific audience (e.g. a parliamentary submission, a community presentation, a letter to a local councillor) and evaluate how audience shapes argument construction

response_modes.reason: Evidence incorporation is an integration task — students must combine their civic content knowledge, their source evaluation skills (AC9HC9S02), and their perspective analysis skills (AC9HC9S03) in the production of a single argument. Feedback on drafts that distinguishes evidence integration from evidence reference is the key teaching move.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Argument construction that addresses counter-arguments and tailors evidence to audience are hallmarks of sophisticated civic literacy. Advancing students who develop multiple argument types (written submission, oral advocacy, visual argument) across different civic contexts are building transferable capabilities for democratic participation.
success_criteria: Constructs an argument on a civic issue that includes at least one claim and one piece of supporting evidence
Evidence is integrated into the argument (supports a claim) rather than simply listed or appended
Uses at least two civics and citizenship terms accurately within the argument
